newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wheat exports to Iraq in limbo.
newsitem.headline: Australian wheat exports to Iraq in limbo.

text.p: The potential for Australia to start shipments of old crop wheat to Iraq with the suspension of the oil-for-food deal were quickly diminishing, James Price, Australian Wheat Board (AWB) manager grower relations, said.
"It's all in limbo for the moment," Price told Reuters.

Price was commenting on the opportunity for Australia to re-enter the major Iraq wheat market through oil-for-food deals announced in July which could have been worth a total of US$200 million a year in Australian wheat exports.
UN oil-for-food deals for Iraq were supended on Tuesday after the U.S. missile attack on Iraq.
Australia hoped to be able to ship new crop wheat to Iraq later, depending on UN resolutions, Price said.
Before suspension of the oil-for-food deal, the AWB expected to begin shipping wheat to Iraq at the rate of 100,000 tonnes a month this spring, he said.
"Clearly that's very much an outside chance at the moment," Price said.

Iraq had been an important customer for Australian wheat, regularly taking up to one million tonnes a year, before the Gulf War. Since the Gulf War, Australian wheat shipments have been only very small tonnages.
The oil-for-food deal had provided the opportunity for Australia to get back into the Iraq market in a significant way. "I guess we'll just have to wait and see how things unfold," Price said.
The oil-for-food was up for the UN's signature but had not been signed before the suspension, he said.
One of the main issues was that UN inspectors were to have been in Iraq making sure food imported under the oil-for-food deal reached where it was supposed to go.
"Clearly with the conflict their security would not be able to be guaranteed," Price said.
A precise starting date for exports of Australian wheat to Iraq under the oil-for-food deal had not been set, pending formal UN clearance of the agreement and distribution arrangements, Price said.
Australia's initial wheat export agreement was for four to six months, limiting the potential value of exports in the first year to less than US$200 million worth.
Performance of the deal also depended on resolution of details and logistical difficulties, Price said.
"It was really all a matter of feeling our way and seeing how it went," he said.
But Price would not downplay the impact of suspension of the oil-for-food deal on Australia's national wheat sales.
"Clearly a customer with the ability to take 100,000 tonnes a month is a significant one," he said.
The world wheat market was presently finely balanced with low world stocks and relatively high prices, he said.
Increased world production would result from high prices but Australia was confident about the market, he said.
The oil-for-food deal would have allowed Iraq to sell US$2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
